games.explanation: Luzardo is a nightmare for lefties and merely a good pitcher against righties, and the Marlins happen to trot out a righty-heavy lineup built to make his life difficult. Stowers in particular has been mashing right-handed pitching all year with a .395 xwOBA, and Hernandez brings the kind of barrel rate that plays in any park with the roof shut. Gusto is nobody's idea of an ace, but the sim has this as a one-run game and the market has it priced like Philly is the clear side. Two evenly matched teams by Elo, a starter matchup that tightens once you separate the platoons, and you're getting +145 on the coin flip.

Toronto's rookie flamethrower has been quietly getting hammered by right-handed bats, and Washington happens to run out a lineup full of them at the top of the order. Yesavage's numbers against lefties look like a Cy Young case, but flip the split and righties are punishing him with a barrel rate north of eleven percent and hard contact on nearly two-thirds of balls in play. James Wood and Luis García Jr. are exactly the kind of righty bats built to exploit that gap, and Littell's contact-management profile plays fine in a park that doesn't reward the fly balls Yesavage is prone to giving up. Getting a coin-flip price on the team our numbers make a clear favorite is the entire ballgame at +100.

Cleveland is being priced like the obvious side in a game that projects as a coin flip, and coin flips at plus money are how you get paid. Brady Singer walks too many hitters to be a comfortable favorite, and this Reds lineup gets Elly De La Cruz and a hot Sal Stewart into the box against right-handed pitching where they do their real damage. The park is a bandbox that punishes exactly Singer's contact profile, with a home run factor north of 1.30 turning warning-track outs into swing plays. Kwan and Ramirez are lovely hitters, but neither one hits the ball hard enough to run away with a game like this. +116 on the better roster in a live-scoring environment is the whole story.

Dustin May is being priced like a competent mid-rotation arm, which is generous for a righty who walks nearly six percent more hitters than he strikes out against left-handed bats. The Cubs happen to run out a lineup full of them, and Busch in particular has been abusing right-handed pitching all year to the tune of a .403 xwOBA. Boyd is quietly the better arm in this game by a comfortable margin, missing more bats and giving up softer contact than anything May has managed. When the market makes you lay less than even money on the better team with the better starter, you take it and move on.

The market is pricing this like Minnesota is the clearly better team pushing around a lesser opponent, but the simulation has these two playing to a dead heat at the final buzzer. Joe Ryan is a legitimate strikeout arm, though the lefty side of his splits is where the barrels live, and Kansas City happens to run a stack of left-handed bats through the top of the order. Salvy adds the right-handed thump against a pitcher whose xwOBA doesn't quite match the shiny surface numbers, and the park is playing generous tonight even with the wind blowing in. Getting a run and a half at -137 in a projected 4-4 fight is the kind of price you take and stop overthinking.

Boston is the better team, nobody's arguing that, but the run line is doing all the work the moneyline can't quite justify. The sim spits out a one-run game because Jacob Lopez misses bats at a starter-plus rate and the Athletics run a lineup deep enough to trade haymakers, with Kurtz and Soderstrom both carrying xwOBAs that play anywhere. A neutral park and a projected 4.7 to 4.8 final is not the profile of a laugher, it's the profile of a bullpen game that ends 5-4 either way. Getting -118 to lose by exactly one or win outright is the entire pitch, and the market is still pricing this like a mismatch.
